g10-geography-ug2-t1.overview: Climate is the long-term average of weather, and classifying it lets geographers describe a whole region in two or three terms. This lesson defines climate against weather, traces world climate classification from the ancient Greeks to Koppen, and maps the four major global climate zones by latitude.
objectives: Define climate and distinguish it from weather
Explain why climate classification is useful in daily life
Describe the ancient Greek and modern schemes of climate classification
Identify Koppen's principal climate groups and the criterion that defines each one
Locate and characterise the four major global climate zones by latitude
g10-geography-ug2-t1.simple: Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, thirty years or more, while weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere on a single day. Climatic zones are spacious, belt-shaped areas with similar climates that spread east and west around the Earth. The ancient Greeks made the first classification, dividing each hemisphere into torrid, temperate and frigid zones. The most widely used modern scheme belongs to Koppen, who grouped world climates as A humid tropical, B dry, C mild-winter middle latitude, D severe-winter middle latitude, E polar, and H highland. Four great global zones exist by latitude: the tropical zone from 0 to 23.5 degrees, the subtropics from 23.5 to 40 degrees, the temperate zone from 40 to 60 degrees, and the cold zone from 60 to 90 degrees.
g10-geography-ug2-t1.detailed:
Climate versus weather. Climate is an average of weather conditions in a place over a long period, thirty years or more; it represents the sum of all interacting atmospheric processes over a given period. Weather, on the other hand, refers to a short-term atmospheric condition - the temperature and precipitation on a certain day, the state of the atmosphere with respect to heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness.

Climatic zones and regions. Climatic zones are spacious areas with a climatic similarity; they spread in an east-west direction around the Earth and are belt-shaped and circular around the poles, though mountains or oceans can interrupt them. A climatic region is a continuous geographic area in which similar climate characteristics are observed. Average temperature is the most important factor in determining climate regions of the world, although other weather aspects like precipitation play roles.

Why classify climates? Classifications help people know what conditions a region usually experiences through the year, communicating expected conditions in just two or three terms instead of describing every month. Knowing a region's classification is useful when choosing building materials for protection and durability, when considering which crops are likely to thrive, and for tourists selecting and packing appropriate clothing.

From the Greeks to modern schemes. Perhaps the first attempt was made by the ancient Greeks, who divided each hemisphere into three zones: torrid (tropical), temperate and frigid. Since the beginning of the twentieth century many schemes have been devised using long-term records of temperature and precipitation, with names such as polar, tropical, continental and marine, modified by descriptors like moist or dry, warm or cold, and temperate or severe. Today scientists split the Earth into approximately five major types - tropical, dry, temperate, continental and polar - considering altitude, air pressure, wind patterns, latitude and geographical characteristics such as mountains and oceans.

Koppen's classification. The most widely used scheme was made by the German climatologist and botanist Wladimir Koppen (1846-1940), who divided world climates into categories based on general temperature profiles related to latitude, using easily obtained mean monthly and annual values of temperature and precipitation. Koppen believed the distribution of natural vegetation was the best expression of an overall climate. He recognised five principal groups, each with a capital letter: A (humid tropical), B (dry), C (humid middle-latitude, mild winters), D (humid middle-latitude, severe winters), E (polar) and H (highland). Four groups (A, C, D, E) are defined by temperature, group B has precipitation as its primary criterion, and H is determined by altitude.

The four global climate zones. The Earth's climate is driven by energy from the sun. Sunlight reaches the ground almost perpendicularly at the equator, while at the poles the angle is low or even below the horizon during the polar night; the noon angle varies from perpendicular (90 degrees) within the tropics up to horizontal (0 degrees) within the polar circle, so the equator is warmed much more strongly. The four zones are: the Tropical Zone from 0 to 23.5 degrees, where radiation is nearly vertical, it is very warm, evaporation is high and frequent dense cloud cover reduces the effect of solar radiation on ground temperature; the Subtropics Zone from 23.5 to 40 degrees, which receives the highest summer radiation with a relatively thin cloud cover and little moisture, so most of the world's deserts lie here; the Temperate Zone from 40 to 60 degrees, with cooler temperatures, significantly differing seasons and day length, more regular precipitation and a longer vegetation period; and the Cold Zone from 60 to 90 degrees, where the low sun angle gives little heat, day length varies most (polar days occur in summer), vegetation is possible only during a few months and life is very challenging.

Altitude modifies the zones. The characteristics of climate zones change with great altitude differences within a small area, like in mountain areas, since temperatures decrease rapidly with altitude.

keyTerms.def: An average of weather conditions in a place over a long period, thirty years or more; the sum of all interacting atmospheric processes over a given period.
The short-term atmospheric condition of a certain day - heat or cold, wetness or dryness, calm or storm, clearness or cloudiness.
A spacious belt-shaped area with climatic similarity, spreading east and west around the Earth.
A continuous geographic area in which similar climate characteristics are observed.
A scheme that communicates a region's expected conditions using just two or three terms.
The widely used scheme by Wladimir Koppen (1846-1940) grouping climates as A humid tropical, B dry, C mild-winter middle latitude, D severe-winter middle latitude, E polar and H highland.
A description of the climate of the Earth as a whole, with all regional differences averaged.
The period near the poles when the sun stays under the horizon, so the solar angle is low or absent.

workedExamples.problem: A weather station's long-term records give monthly mean temperatures of 24, 25, 26, 27, 26, 24, 23, 23, 24, 25, 25 and 25 degrees C. Work out its mean annual temperature, the key figure for naming a climate region.
workedExamples.given: Twelve monthly mean temperatures from long-term records.
workedExamples.formula: Mean annual temperature = (sum of the 12 monthly means) / 12
workedExamples.answer: About 24.8 degrees C - a warm station of tropical type, since climate is judged from long-term averages.

workedExamples.problem: Place each station in its global climate zone by latitude: M at 8 degrees N, N at 31 degrees S, O at 47 degrees N, P at 78 degrees N.
workedExamples.given: Zone boundaries: tropical 0-23.5 degrees, subtropics 23.5-40 degrees, temperate 40-60 degrees, cold 60-90 degrees.
workedExamples.formula: Match each latitude to the zone whose range contains it.
workedExamples.substitution: 8 falls in 0-23.5; 31 falls in 23.5-40; 47 falls in 40-60; 78 falls in 60-90.
workedExamples.calculation: Each latitude is inside exactly one zone range.
workedExamples.answer: M - Tropical Zone; N - Subtropics Zone; O - Temperate Zone; P - Cold Zone.

workedExamples.problem: Identify Koppen's principal group for each area: (i) a warm, humid lowland near the equator; (ii) a humid mid-latitude area with severe winters; (iii) a cool high mountain area such as the Ethiopian highlands.
workedExamples.given: Groups: A humid tropical; B dry; C humid middle latitude with mild winters; D humid middle latitude with severe winters; E polar; H highland.
workedExamples.formula: Match each description to the criterion that defines the group - temperature, precipitation or altitude.
workedExamples.substitution: (i) is humid and tropical; (ii) is humid middle latitude with severe winters; (iii) is defined by altitude.
workedExamples.calculation: A, C, D and E are temperature groups, B is the precipitation group and H is the altitude group.

commonMistakes: Using 'weather' and 'climate' interchangeably; weather is a single day's atmospheric condition, while climate is a 30-year or longer average.
Forgetting the basis of Koppen's letters: A, C, D and E rest on temperature, B on precipitation and H on altitude.
Placing the temperate zone between 23.5 and 40 degrees when that range is the subtropics.
Believing the sun warms the equator and the poles equally; the noon angle falls from about 90 degrees in the tropics to 0 degrees at the polar circle.
Overlooking that mountains and oceans interrupt the belt-shaped climate zones in some areas.
Thinking dense equatorial cloud cover heats the ground more, when it actually reduces the effect of solar radiation on ground temperature.
applications: Reading Ethiopia's latitude, roughly 3 to 15 degrees N, to explain why its lowlands stay warm all year round.
Using altitude to explain why the Ethiopian highlands are cool while nearby lowlands at the same latitude are hot.
Helping a farmer choose crops by matching the local climate classification to what crops are likely to thrive in the region.
Advising a family on what clothing to pack for a journey by consulting the destination's climate zone.
Choosing durable building materials for a school or house from the region's expected conditions instead of guessing.
g10-geography-ug2-t1.summary: Climate is the 30-year-or-more average of weather, while weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere on a given day. Classifications let two or three terms communicate a region's expected conditions, and Koppen's scheme - built on temperature, precipitation and altitude - is the most widely used. The four global zones, tropical, subtropics, temperate and cold, arise because the sun warms the equator far more strongly than the poles, with altitude adding local variation.

g10-geography-ug2-t2.overview: Africa's position across the equator and both tropics makes it the most tropical of all continents and gives it a nearly mirror-image arrangement of climate zones north and south of the equator. This lesson maps the continent's climatic regions, from the equatorial belt to the Mediterranean fringes, and the five factors that control them.
objectives: Locate Africa in tropical latitudes and explain the effect of that position
Identify the major climatic regions of Africa and characterise each one
Describe the seasonal movement of the ITCZ and the trade winds it generates
Explain how ocean currents, the distribution of land and water, and altitude control climate
Match African localities and data clues to their climatic regions
g10-geography-ug2-t2.simple: Africa lies almost entirely within the tropics: the equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn all cross the continent, making Africa the most tropical of all continents, with climate zones arranged almost as a mirror image north and south of the equator. Its climates include the equatorial, tropical wet-and-dry, tropical monsoon, semi-arid, hot desert and subtropical highland types, with Mediterranean conditions confined to the far fringes; rainfall is more variable than temperature, which stays consistently high. The movement of air masses divides the continent into climatic regions, including the equatorial, tropical wet-and-dry, semi-arid, hot desert, humid subtropical, Mediterranean, warm temperate east coast, warm temperate continental and mountain regions. Latitude, pressure systems and winds with the ITCZ, ocean currents, land and water distribution, and altitude control the whole pattern.
g10-geography-ug2-t2.detailed:
Africa's position and its consequence. Africa straddles the equator from about 37 degrees N to 34 degrees S, and the equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn all cross the continent, making Africa the most tropical of all continents. Its position is relatively unique because it almost has a mirror image of climate zones to the north and south of the equator. Precipitation intensity is always high and it is a hot continent; warm and hot climates prevail, but the northern part is marked by aridity and high temperatures, and only the northernmost and southernmost fringes have a Mediterranean climate. African deserts are the sunniest and driest parts of the continent, owing to the prevailing subtropical ridge with subsiding, hot, dry air masses.

The Equatorial (Tropical Wet) Climate Region. This climate is experienced in the lowland areas between latitudes 5 degrees N and 5 degrees S, covering mainly Central Africa - the Democratic Republic of Congo, Gabon and Cameroon - and the southern parts of Nigeria, Ghana, Benin and Sierra Leone. Temperatures are very high throughout the year, averaging about 26 degrees C; the hottest months are March and September, when the sun is overhead at the equator. The diurnal temperature range is very low, about 3 degrees C, cloud cover is often heavy, humidity is high all year, and the region mainly receives convectional rainfall. Highland and coastal areas of Eastern Africa experience a modified equatorial climate with much lower temperatures.

The Tropical Wet-and-Dry (Savanna) Region. This region covers a little less than half of the total surface area of the continent. Its great distinguishing feature is the seasonal character of its rainfall: during the period of high sun, maritime air masses produce up to six months of rainfall, and the rest of the year is dry. In western Africa the period of low sun corresponds to the harmattan season - a warm, dry, northeasterly or easterly wind blowing out of the southern Sahara, frequently laden with large quantities of sand and dust. Regions with an equatorial or tropical wet climate are the wettest in Africa, with two rainfall peaks corresponding to the double passage of the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone. A notable variation occurs on the western coast from around Cape Three Points in Ghana eastward to Benin, where the regime is bimodal but the annual total is under 1,000 mm, because cold offshore water chills and stabilises the maritime air, winds blow parallel to the shore and no highlands supply orographic rainfall. In Eastern Africa the tropical type is experienced in Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania and Somalia; in Central Africa in Zambia, Malawi, Angola, Namibia, Botswana and Zimbabwe.

Semi-arid and Hot Desert Regions. The semi-arid region fringes the desert areas and includes the greater part of the land south of the Zambezi River; it lies just within reach of the ITCZ in its seasonal movement, so it receives somewhat more rainfall than true desert, at similar temperatures. The hot desert region consists of the Sahara and Kalahari deserts, always under dry continental tropical air masses, and the northern Kenya-Somali desert, whose aridity comes mainly from the stable nature of maritime air masses chilled by passing over the cool offshore water. Desert days are extremely hot, usually between 30 and 40 degrees C, and some places in the Sahara exceed 40 degrees C; the highest temperature ever recorded there and in the world was 58 degrees C at Azizia, Libya. At night temperatures drop below 10 degrees C because clear skies let the daytime heat escape, so the diurnal range is greater than the annual range of the mean monthly temperatures.

Mediterranean, Humid Subtropical and Warm Temperate Regions. The Mediterranean climate, also called Warm Temperate Western Margin, is best developed on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea and also occurs at the south-western tip of Africa; temperatures range from about 10 degrees C in winter to about 21 degrees C in summer, summers are dry as winds blow from land to sea, winters are wet and mild under cool moist westerlies, and annual rainfall averages about 500-750 mm. At the northern and southern extremities rain falls only in winter - December-January in North Africa, June-July in Southern Africa. The humid subtropical climate, a transition between tropical and temperate climates found on eastern continental sides between 20 and 35 degrees latitude, is confined in Africa to the southeastern coast of South Africa and appears in Koppen's scheme as Cfa and Cwa. The Warm Temperate East Coast climate, between 30 and 40 degrees on both sides of the equator, occurs along the eastern coast of South Africa, especially in Natal and Cape Provinces, and in Mozambique; influenced by the warm Mozambique current and the warm southeast trade winds, summers average about 26 degrees C, winters about 10 degrees C, and rainfall of 1000-1500 mm per year decreases westwards into the interior. The Warm Temperate Continental climate occupies the interior of South Africa between the Drakensberg Mountains and the Kalahari Desert; rainfall is low (about 700 mm, mostly in winter) because winds from the sea arrive already dry, the east is wetter than the west, and temperatures range from about 26 degrees C in summer to about 10 degrees C in winter.

The Mountain Climatic Region. This region includes the high mountain areas of Kenya, Ethiopia and the lakes region of East Africa. Temperatures are even lower than in the warm temperate upland climate, and snow occurs on the tops of the highest peaks, such as Kilimanjaro. The area receives more rainfall than its surroundings, mostly relief rainfall formed as warm moist winds are forced to rise up the highlands; the windward slopes receive the highest amounts, while the leeward, rain-shadow slopes facing away from the sea receive little or no rain from the descending winds. Temperature decreases as altitude increases, and at the very top of high mountains temperatures fall below freezing point.

Factors controlling Africa's climate. Latitude: because Africa spans 37 degrees N to 34 degrees S and lies within the tropics, temperature is high throughout; as latitude increases the sun shines more obliquely and provides less energy. Pressure, winds and the ITCZ: subtropical high-pressure belts near 30 degrees N and S generate the Northeast Trade Winds, locally called the Harmattan - dry and cool, blowing over Sub-Saharan Africa from about November to April - and the Southwest Trade Winds, locally called the Monsoon, which are moist and bring rainfall to the coasts of West Africa; the two wind systems converge at the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, which sits at about 13 degrees north, at the southern boundary of the Sahara, in June, and moves southward in December along the West African coast and to the northern and eastern margins of the Congo basin and on to Madagascar. Ocean currents: warm currents such as the Guinea Current in West Africa and the Mozambique Current in the southeast supply moisture that falls as rain on adjacent coasts, while cool currents such as the Canary Current, off the western coast of the Sahara, and the Benguela Current, off the western coast of the Kalahari, chill the winds so they absorb rather than deposit moisture, causing dry conditions - though they create rich fishing grounds off Morocco, the Spanish Saharan coasts and Namibia. Distribution of land and water: continental interiors heat rapidly by day and cool rapidly at night, giving continental climates with extreme ranges - at Timbuktu in Mali the diurnal and annual temperature ranges are very high - while coasts have maritime climates. Altitude: air temperature decreases with altitude at an average rate of 6.4 degrees C per 1000 meters, the Lapse Rate, which is why the Ethiopian highlands are cool and very high equatorial peaks such as Kilimanjaro carry permanent snow.

keyTerms.def: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds from the two subtropical high-pressure belts converge near the equator; its seasonal movement governs much of Africa's rainfall.
The locally named Northeast Trade Wind - dry and cool, blowing from the southern Sahara over Sub-Saharan Africa from about November to April, often laden with sand and dust.
The local name in Africa for the moist Southwest Trade Winds that bring rainfall to the coasts of West Africa.
A current flowing from low toward high latitudes; it supplies moisture to winds, developing rainfall on adjacent coasts, as with the Guinea and Mozambique currents.
A current whose cold surface chills winds so they absorb rather than deposit moisture, causing dry conditions and fog; it creates rich fishing grounds, as with the Canary and Benguela currents.
Rain from intense heating that makes moist air rise, cool and release heavy showers; the main type in the equatorial region.
Orographic rain formed when warm moist winds are forced to rise up highlands; the windward slopes receive the highest amounts.
The leeward slope facing away from the sea, which receives little or no rain because the descending winds have lost their moisture.

workedExamples.problem: A highland station stands 2,500 metres above a nearby lowland whose air temperature is 25 degrees C. Using the average rate at which temperature falls with height, estimate the highland's temperature.
workedExamples.given: Altitude difference 2,500 m; lowland temperature 25 degrees C; average lapse rate 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m.
workedExamples.formula: Temperature drop = lapse rate x (altitude difference / 1000)
workedExamples.answer: About 9 degrees C - air temperature decreases with altitude at an average of 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m.

workedExamples.problem: Station X lies at low altitude near the equator: mean temperature about 26 degrees C, diurnal range about 3 degrees C, heavy cloud, high humidity and mainly convectional rain. Name its African climatic region.
workedExamples.given: Mean about 26 degrees C; diurnal range about 3 degrees C; heavy cloud; convectional rainfall.
workedExamples.formula: Compare the observed characteristics with the defining features of each climatic region.
workedExamples.substitution: The equatorial region is defined by about 26 degrees C averages, a very low diurnal range and mainly convectional rainfall.
workedExamples.calculation: The features coincide exactly with the Equatorial (Tropical Wet) Region found between about 5 degrees N and 5 degrees S in Central Africa.

workedExamples.problem: Two ships follow the same wind belt: one sails over the cool Canary Current toward the western Sahara coast, one over the warm Guinea Current toward the Guinea coast. Compare the expected coastal climate effects.
workedExamples.given: Warm currents supply moisture to winds and develop rainfall on adjacent coasts; cool currents chill winds so they absorb rather than deposit moisture.
workedExamples.formula: Classify each current as warm or cool, then apply its moisture effect on the adjacent coast.
workedExamples.substitution: Canary = cool, off the western Sahara coast; Guinea = warm, in West Africa.
workedExamples.calculation: Winds over the cool current stay dry and form fogs, so the coast stays arid; winds over the warm current carry moisture that falls as coastal rainfall.
workedExamples.answer: The Canary side is dry but has rich fishing grounds off Morocco and the Spanish Saharan coasts; the Guinea side receives moist winds and heavier coastal rainfall.

workedExamples.problem: Identify the African climatic region for each clue: (i) the greater part of the land south of the Zambezi River, just within reach of the ITCZ; (ii) shores with mild wet winters and dry hot summers, about 500-750 mm of rain; (iii) high East African mountains with snow on the highest peaks.
workedExamples.given: Regions include the semi-arid, Mediterranean and mountain climatic regions.
workedExamples.formula: Match each location clue to the named characteristics of the region.
workedExamples.substitution: (i) fringes the desert and gains extra rain from the ITCZ; (ii) lies in the path of moist westerly winds with winter rain; (iii) temperatures fall below freezing on the highest tops.
workedExamples.calculation: Each clue is one of the textbook's defining statements for a named region.
workedExamples.answer: (i) Semi-arid Climatic Region; (ii) Mediterranean Climate Region; (iii) Mountain Climatic Region.

commonMistakes: Treating Africa as uniformly hot and wet; rainfall is far more variable than temperature, and the northern part of the continent is marked by aridity.
Assuming tropical wet-and-dry climate covers every savanna-vegetated area; the name implies, incorrectly, that all such areas share this climate.
Blaming distance from the sea for the northern Kenya-Somali desert; its aridity comes mainly from stable maritime air masses chilled over the cool offshore water.
Claiming the harmattan brings rain; it is warm, dry, and frequently laden with sand and dust.
Swapping the effects of warm and cool ocean currents; warm currents feed coastal rainfall, while cool currents cause dryness but create rich fishing grounds.
Misquoting the lapse rate; temperature falls about 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m of altitude, not per 100 m.
Forgetting that in hot deserts the diurnal temperature range is greater than the annual range of the mean monthly temperatures.
applications: Predicting wet and dry months for Ethiopian farming by tracking the ITCZ, which stays near 13 degrees N in June and retreats southward in December.
Explaining the fogs and rich fishing grounds off Morocco, the Spanish Saharan coasts and Namibia through the cool Canary and Benguela currents.
Using a Koppen map of Africa to match real places - for example the south-western tip of Africa with its Mediterranean climate.
Applying the lapse rate of 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m to explain why the Ethiopian highlands stay cool and Kilimanjaro keeps permanent snow.
Explaining the extreme temperature ranges of continental interiors such as Timbuktu in Mali through continentality.
Guiding settlement and water storage plans by locating an area's region - south of the Zambezi, the desert belts, or the equatorial lowlands.
g10-geography-ug2-t2.summary: Africa's span across the equator and both tropics, plus its mirror-image symmetry about the equator, produces equatorial, tropical wet-and-dry, semi-arid, hot desert, humid subtropical, Mediterranean, warm temperate and mountain climatic regions. Five controls shape the pattern: latitude, the subtropical high-pressure systems and trade winds with the shifting ITCZ, warm and cool ocean currents, the distribution of land and water, and altitude, whose lapse rate of 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m cools the highlands.

questions.q: Africa is called the most tropical of all continents because:
options: its climate is always hot everywhere
the equator and both tropics run through it
all of it lies south of the equator
questions.explanation: The equator, the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn all run through Africa.

questions.q: The climate of Africa is more variable in rainfall amount than in temperature.
questions.explanation: African temperatures are consistently high, but rainfall amounts vary greatly.

questions.q: Name the Libyan station that recorded the highest temperature ever measured in the region and in the world: 58 degrees C.
questions.explanation: The record of 58 degrees C was set at Azizia, Libya.

questions.q: The harmattan is best described as:
options: a warm, dry, northeasterly wind from the southern Sahara, often laden with sand and dust
the rainy monsoon of East Africa
questions.explanation: The harmattan is a warm, dry northeasterly or easterly wind blowing out of the southern Sahara.

questions.q: Give two reasons why the western African coast from Cape Three Points in Ghana eastward to Benin receives less than 1,000 mm of rain.
questions.answer: cold offshore water chills and stabilises the maritime air|winds blow parallel to the shore|no highlands give orographic rain
questions.explanation: Cold offshore water makes the lower maritime air stable, winds tend to blow parallel to the shore, and the absence of highlands deprives the region of orographic rainfall.

questions.q: Which current helps keep the western Sahara coast dry but also creates rich fishing grounds?
questions.explanation: The cool Canary Current off the western coast of the Sahara causes dry conditions and supports rich fishing grounds off Morocco and the Spanish Saharan coasts.

questions.q: Cool ocean currents tend to create rich fishing grounds.
questions.explanation: The cool Canary and Benguela currents create rich fishing grounds off Morocco, the Spanish Saharan coasts and the Namibian coast.

questions.q: A place has mild wet winters brought by moist westerly winds, dry hot summers and annual rainfall of about 500-750 mm. Its climatic region is:
questions.explanation: Mild wet winters under westerlies with 500-750 mm per year define the Mediterranean climate region.

questions.q: Name the two deserts that make up the hot desert climatic region of Africa.
questions.answer: Sahara and Kalahari|the Sahara and the Kalahari
questions.explanation: The hot desert region consists of the Sahara and Kalahari deserts, under dry continental tropical air masses.

questions.q: Using the lapse rate, explain why the highest East African peaks carry snow despite lying near the equator.
questions.answer: temperature falls about 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m so the peaks are below freezing|altitude lowers temperature below freezing point
questions.explanation: Air temperature decreases with altitude at an average rate of 6.4 degrees C per 1000 m, so the very high tops fall below freezing point.

questions.q: Arrange these climatic regions in the order they appear moving southward from the equator across southern Africa.
questions.explanation: Moving southward the sequence is equatorial, tropical wet-and-dry, hot desert, then the Mediterranean fringes - Africa's mirror-image symmetry about the equator.

g10-geography-ug2-t3.overview: Climate reaches into almost every part of African life, from food and transport to settlement, health and water. This lesson connects Africa's climate types to agriculture, human health and water supply, and shows why the continent's economy rests so heavily on its climate.
objectives: Explain how climate shapes settlement patterns and livelihood options
Describe the role of climate in African agriculture using key figures
Relate climate events such as floods and droughts to human health outcomes
Explain the link between climate and surface-water supply in Africa
Debate both the benefits and the disadvantages of climate for African life
g10-geography-ug2-t3.simple: Climate affects nearly every aspect of life: food sources, transport infrastructure, clothing, recreation, livelihood, health and the future. Places with better climates draw dense settlement, while deserts, rainforests and polar regions hold few people. Agriculture, the backbone of Africa's economy, accounts on average for about 70 percent of the labour force and over 25 percent of GDP, and the bulk of Sub-Saharan farming depends directly on rain, so a steady mixture of sun, warmth and rains decides every harvest. Climate also shapes health: floods cause drownings, droughts lead to crop failure and hunger, and temperature extremes pose a risk of exposure. Finally water, the most important of all natural resources, depends on climate, because stream levels, river flow and the volume of underground water all follow rainfall and temperature.
g10-geography-ug2-t3.detailed:
Climate and daily life. Climate affects nearly every aspect of our lives, from our food sources to our transport infrastructure, from what clothes we wear to where we go for recreation; it has a huge effect on our livelihood, our health and our future. People's settlement and living are hugely associated with climate types: some places are overpopulated due to better climate and associated factors, while regions of extreme climatic conditions such as the deserts, rainforests and polar regions have fewer people.

The diversity of Africa's climate landscape. Africa is a continent with a diversity of climate landscapes, ranging from intense heat to bitter cold in its different parts. This diversity influences the living style of people, including settlement patterns, livelihood options, resource endowments, health and wellbeing. Understanding the relationship between climate, physical resources and the socio-economic conditions of people is therefore central to understanding Africa.

Climate and agriculture. Agriculture is the backbone of Africa's economy and accounts for the majority of livelihoods across the continent, on average about 70 percent of the labour force and over 25 percent of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Agriculture has always been deeply dependent on the weather, with farmers needing a steady mixture of sun, warmth and rains to reliably produce their crops. The bulk of agricultural systems in Sub-Saharan Africa are highly climate-dependent, marked by a strong dependence on rain-fed agriculture and natural resources. Africa is among the continents most highly affected by climate change for two reasons: its geographical position across the warming tropics, and the limited human, social and economic capacity of its countries to adapt. A change of climate therefore worsens existing difficulties, such as few technological inputs, the fact that most of Africa's farmers work on a small-scale or subsistence level with few financial resources, and limited access to infrastructure.

Climate and health. Humans have understood the importance of climate to health since ancient times. Some connections are obvious: a flood can cause drownings, a drought can lead to crop failure and hunger, and temperature extremes pose a risk of exposure. Other connections are obscured by complex or unobserved processes, so the influence of climate on a disease epidemic or a conflict can be difficult to diagnose. In reality, all climate impacts on health are mediated by some combination of natural and human dynamics that make individuals or populations vulnerable. Africa is commonly described as a 'climate-vulnerable' continent, in which rainfall variability, hydrological extremes and anthropogenic climate change have the potential to inflict significant harm on a large population.

Climate and water resources. Water is the most important of all natural resources; without it, life would not be able to thrive on the Earth. The level of streams, the flow of streams and rivers, and the volume of underground water all depend on types of climates and water availability. Therefore persistent climate change may lead to shrinkage in the surface-water supply, in the quantity and regularity of streams and rivers, and in water supplies in Africa.

Weighing benefits and burdens. The influence of climate on human activities can be both positive and negative. On the positive side, warm temperatures and seasonal rains support crops, natural vegetation, fishing and tourism, and favourable climates attract dense settlement. On the negative side, droughts, floods and temperature extremes destroy harvests, endanger health and push people off the land, especially where farming depends on rain alone.

workedExamples.problem: A development survey covers 500 working people in a Sub-Saharan district. Given agriculture's average share of Africa's labour force, how many of these livelihoods depend on agriculture?
workedExamples.given: Total surveyed = 500; agriculture employs on average about 70 percent of Africa's labour force.
workedExamples.formula: Number depending on agriculture = total x share / 100
workedExamples.answer: About 350 of the 500 livelihoods - evidence of how strongly African life is tied to climate-dependent farming.

workedExamples.problem: A district receives one wet season of up to six months during the period of high sun and a long dry season in the period of low sun, when the harmattan blows. Name the climatic region and state what it means for rain-fed farming.
workedExamples.given: A rainy season of up to six months when maritime air masses dominate, then a dry season; the harmattan marks the period of low sun.
workedExamples.formula: Match the seasonal rainfall pattern to the defining feature of each climatic region.
workedExamples.substitution: The pattern - seasonal character of rainfall over roughly half the year - matches the tropical wet-and-dry (savanna climatic) region.
workedExamples.calculation: Planting must fit inside the wet season; the dry season demands storage and drought measures because the harvest depends on the rains.
workedExamples.answer: The district lies in the tropical wet-and-dry region; rain-fed farming succeeds only if planting follows the rains closely.

workedExamples.problem: Map the health chain that follows when the rains fail in a rain-dependent African district.
workedExamples.given: A rainless growing season; rain-fed farming; thin household food reserves.
workedExamples.formula: Follow the climate-to-health chain: climate event, then livelihood effect, then health effect.
workedExamples.substitution: Rains fail, then crops fail, then hunger follows; the parallel chains are floods leading to drownings and temperature extremes posing risk of exposure.
workedExamples.calculation: Each climate event transmits directly into a health outcome through the livelihood step.
workedExamples.answer: Failed rains cause crop failure, which leads to hunger and health harm - climate and health are directly linked.

commonMistakes: Claiming climate has only negative effects; its influence on human activities can be both positive and negative, with warmth and rains as benefits.
Assuming most Sub-Saharan farming is irrigated; it is marked by a strong dependence on rain-fed agriculture and natural resources.
Believing settlement has nothing to do with climate; dense populations cluster in better climates while deserts, rainforests and polar regions hold few people.
Thinking every climate-health link is instantly visible; some, such as the influence of climate on a disease epidemic or a conflict, are obscured by complex processes.
Blaming only the weather for poor harvests while ignoring the structural weaknesses: few technological inputs, small-scale subsistence farming, few financial resources and limited infrastructure.
Forgetting the link between climate and water; stream levels, river flow and underground water volumes all track the type of climate.
applications: Explaining why Ethiopia's better-watered highlands are densely settled while the extreme lowland deserts and dry margins hold fewer people.
Timing planting and harvesting to fit the rainy season of a tropical wet-and-dry district, since most farming is rain-fed.
Advising a village to store water for the dry season, because streams, rivers and wells shrink when the rains fail.
Interpreting why Ethiopia's GDP - like Africa's, over 25 percent from agriculture - moves with the performance of the rains.
Discussing in class whether the local climate is a net benefit or a risk for crops, health, fishing and settlement.
Linking river flow and well levels in your area to rainfall records, so community water plans follow the climate.
g10-geography-ug2-t3.summary: Climate touches nearly every part of African life - settlement, clothing, transport, livelihood, health and future. Agriculture, the backbone of Africa's economy at about 70 percent of the labour force and over 25 percent of GDP, relies on rain-fed systems, while climate events such as floods, droughts and temperature extremes feed directly into health outcomes, and surface water supplies follow the rainfall regime.

g10-geography-ug2-t4.overview: Climate variability and climate change are related but distinct, and human-caused change has already reached Africa. This lesson separates the two concepts, explains why Africa is among the most vulnerable continents, and analyses how climate change threatens agriculture, water, health, and the MDGs and Africa 2063.
objectives: Distinguish climate variability from climate change
Explain why Africa is among the most vulnerable continents to climate change
Describe the projected impacts of climate change in Africa
Identify evidence that climate change is already happening in Africa
Explain how climate change challenges the MDGs, the Africa 2063 goal and development policies
g10-geography-ug2-t4.simple: Climate variability and climate change are often interchanged, but they differ clearly. Variability may arise from natural internal processes within the climate system or from anthropogenic (human-caused) external forcing, and it occurs with or without our actions. Climate change is a longer-lasting shift in the state of the climate system, persisting typically for decades or longer, due to natural and/or anthropogenic processes and drivers. Africa is among the most vulnerable continents: hundreds of millions of people depend on rainfall to grow their food, adaptive capacity is low, and agricultural production systems are less developed. Projections point to higher temperatures, rising sea levels, changing rainfall patterns and increased variability, with the two most extensive land-based end-of-century decreases in rainfall anywhere on the planet expected over North and South Africa - threatening agriculture, water, health and the achievement of the MDGs and Africa 2063.
g10-geography-ug2-t4.detailed:
Variability is not change. The two terms are often interchanged, but there is a clear demarcation. Climate variability may be due to natural internal processes within the climate system or to variations in anthropogenic (human-caused) external forcing; in other words, climate variations occur with or without our actions, so it is critical to assess precisely which human actions affect climate and which do not. Climate change, on the other hand, is a change in the state of the climate system, identified by changes in the average conditions and the variability of its properties, that persists for an extended period, typically decades or longer, due to natural and/or anthropogenic processes and drivers.

An increasingly serious threat. Climate change is an increasingly serious threat for Africans because Africa is among the most vulnerable continents. Anthropogenic climate change is already a reality in Africa, as it is elsewhere in the world. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the vulnerability of Africa is driven by a range of factors that include weak adaptive capacity, high dependence on ecosystem goods for livelihoods, and less developed agricultural production systems. The risks to agricultural production, food security, water resources and ecosystem services will likely have increasingly severe consequences for lives and sustainable development prospects.

What the projections show. Most studies predict that Africa is likely to experience higher temperatures, rising sea levels, changing rainfall patterns and increased climate variability, all of which could affect much of its population. Many climate models predict negative impacts on agricultural production and food security in large parts of Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA).

Signs it is already happening. Higher temperatures, the drying up of soils, increased pest and disease, shifts in suitable areas for growing crops and livestock, desertification, floods, deforestation and erosion are all signs that climate change is already happening. This makes climate change one of the greatest environmental, social and economic threats facing Africa.

The poorest are hit hardest. The impact of climate change is more serious on the world's poorest countries, most of which are found in Africa. Poor people already live on the frontlines of pollution, disaster, and degradation of resources and land; for them, adaptation is a matter of sheer survival. Unfortunately, despite growing concern, no exact and reliable figures are available to quantify the economic costs of the negative impacts in Africa for either individuals or society as a whole.

Why Africa is hit, and what is at stake. Africa has been seriously affected for several reasons. First, African society is very closely coupled with the climate system: hundreds of millions of people depend on rainfall to grow their food. Second, the African climate system is controlled by an extremely complex mix of large-scale weather systems. Third, the degree of expected climate change is large - the two most extensive land-based end-of-century projected decreases in rainfall anywhere on the planet occur over Africa, particularly in North and South Africa. Finally, the capacity for adaptation to climate change is low. As far as development is concerned, climate change will strongly affect Africa's ability to achieve the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) and the Africa 2063 goal, and its development policies in general, with increased pressure on agriculture, water supply and demand, health, and political stability.

keyTerms.def: Fluctuations in climate due to natural internal processes of the climate system or to anthropogenic external forcing; they occur with or without human action.
A change in the state of the climate system - in average conditions and variability - persisting typically for decades or longer, from natural and/or anthropogenic drivers.
The interacting atmospheric system whose average state describes climate; African society is very closely coupled with it.
Caused by human activity, as in anthropogenic external forcing or anthropogenic climate change.
The ability of a country or people to adjust to the impacts of climate change; in Africa it is weak, which raises vulnerability.
A common description of Africa, where rainfall variability, hydrological extremes and anthropogenic change can harm a large population.
Global development targets whose achievement in Africa is strongly affected by climate change.
Africa's long-term development vision, also strongly impacted by climate change through pressure on agriculture, water, health and political stability.

workedExamples.problem: Decide whether each case is climate variability or climate change: (i) one unusually dry month in an otherwise normal year; (ii) average annual rainfall that falls and then stays lower for thirty years.
workedExamples.given: Variability: short-term fluctuations from natural internal processes or anthropogenic external forcing. Change: a persistent shift of averages and variability, typically decades or longer.
workedExamples.formula: Test duration first, then whether the average conditions of the climate system have shifted.
workedExamples.substitution: (i) is a single short swing with no shift of the mean; (ii) persists for decades and alters the average.
workedExamples.calculation: Short swings that occur with or without our actions are variability; a decade-plus persistent change of the state of the climate system is climate change.

workedExamples.problem: A rain-fed farming kebele depends on growing-season rains, sells almost no surplus, and has no irrigation or early-warning coverage. Assess its vulnerability to climate change using the IPCC drivers of African vulnerability.
workedExamples.given: IPCC drivers: weak adaptive capacity; high dependence on ecosystem goods for livelihoods; less developed agricultural production systems.
workedExamples.formula: Score the community against each of the three drivers.
workedExamples.substitution: Rain dependence = high dependence on ecosystem goods; no irrigation or warning coverage = weak adaptive capacity; subsistence-level selling = less developed production.
workedExamples.calculation: All three drivers are present, so vulnerability is high on every count.
workedExamples.answer: Highly vulnerable - adaptation measures such as water storage, early warnings and improved farming practice are priorities.

workedExamples.problem: Projections identify the two most extensive land-based end-of-century decreases in rainfall anywhere on the planet. Where do they occur, and which development pressures do they intensify?
workedExamples.given: The projections locate both decreases on the African continent.
workedExamples.formula: Recall the projection, then map it onto the sectors named in the development discussion.
workedExamples.substitution: The decreases occur over North and South Africa.
workedExamples.calculation: Less rainfall increases pressure on agriculture, water supply and demand, health and political stability - the same pressures climate change puts on the MDGs and the Africa 2063 goal.
workedExamples.answer: North and South Africa; the pressure lands on agriculture, water, health and political stability.

commonMistakes: Using climate variability and climate change interchangeably; variability occurs with or without human action, while change is a persistent, decade-plus shift.
Claiming climate change is purely natural or purely human-caused; it arises from natural and/or anthropogenic processes and drivers.
Assuming climate change affects all continents equally; Africa is among the most vulnerable because of weak adaptive capacity and heavy dependence on ecosystem goods.
Thinking only farmers feel the effects; pressure also reaches water supply and demand, health and political stability.
Reading the absence of exact economic figures as proof of small costs; no exact and reliable figures exist, yet the impacts are large.
Treating adaptation as optional; for the world's poorest people, most of whom live in Africa, adaptation is a matter of sheer survival.
Confusing a single bad season with the long projected drying, especially the end-of-century rainfall decreases over North and South Africa.
applications: Discussing how Ethiopia's development goals meet climate pressure on agriculture, water and health, as part of the MDGs and Africa 2063.
Auditing your own kebele against the IPCC vulnerability drivers: rain dependence, adaptive capacity and farming systems.
Distinguishing a single failed season from a persistent shift before labelling an event climate change in a community meeting.
Linking tree planting and reduced deforestation in your area to raising adaptive capacity against climate risks.
Explaining why Sub-Saharan Africa's rain-fed agriculture makes food security fragile under changing rainfall patterns.
Weighing what early-warning systems, irrigation and food storage would add to a village's low adaptive capacity.
g10-geography-ug2-t4.summary: Climate variability is a fluctuation - natural or human-forced - while climate change is a persistent, decade-or-longer shift in the state of the climate system. Africa is among the most vulnerable continents because its society is closely coupled with rainfall, its expected degree of change is large, and its adaptive capacity is low. Rising temperatures, shifting rainfall and the projected drying of North and South Africa press hardest on agriculture, water, health and the achievement of the MDGs and Africa 2063.
